corrected_value.title: Talker discrimination by prelingually deaf children with cochlear implants: Preliminary results

decisions.location: Discussion, page 16, lines 894-900 (with task design in Methods, pages 10-11, lines 563-603; empirical tests in Results, pages 13-14, lines 741-765; and full citation in References, page 19, lines 1081-1082)
decisions.quote:
Results from the TD task also replicated findings from the earlier study of deaf children with
CIs carried out by Cleary and Pisoni (2002). They found much better performance on the
fixed-sentence condition than the varied-sentence condition and stronger correlations
between performance on the fixed-sentence condition and several conventional speech
recognition measures. A similar pattern was also found in the error rates for each condition
in the present study with a much stronger response bias for committing false alarms
observed during the more difficult varied-sentence condition.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In Part II of the study, Roman et al. (2017) administer a 4-channel noise-vocoded adaptation of the Talker Discrimination (TD) task modeled after Cleary and Pisoni (2002) (Annals of Otology, Rhinology, & Laryngology 2002; 111(5 Part 2):113-118) using sentence pairs from the Indiana Multi-Talker Sentence Database. In Results (lines 741-765, Table 3) and Discussion (lines 894-900), they empirically test and directly compare three specific findings from Cleary and Pisoni (2002): (1) significantly higher talker-discrimination accuracy in the fixed-sentence condition than in the varied-sentence condition (t(31)=4.76, p<.001), (2) stronger correlations between the fixed-sentence condition and spoken word recognition measures (rs=.49 and .51, p<.01) than for the varied-sentence condition (rs=.39 and .40, p<.05), and (3) a doubled false-alarm rate in the varied-sentence condition relative to the fixed-sentence condition (23.11% vs. 11.54%, t(30)=-.464, p<.001). The sole shipped row (input_row_index '622', Eisenberg et al., 2002, Ear and Hearing, DOI 10.1097/00003446-200210000-00007) investigated lexically controlled word and sentence recognition and did not include talker discrimination, so report equivalence does not apply and Cleary and Pisoni (2002) is a genuinely absent replication target.

decisions.location: Introduction, page 3, lines 162-167 (and Discussion, page 14, lines 782-794)
decisions.quote:
In
one of their experiments, Eisenberg et al. (2002) assessed the effects of word frequency and
neighborhood density on noise-vocoded word recognition and sentence perception using a
small group of children 5–14 years in age. Eisenberg and colleagues created sets of “easy”
and “hard” words based on manipulations of lexical density and word frequency (see Kirk,
Pisoni, & Osberger, 1995).
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In Part I ('Part I: Replication of Eisenberg et al. (2002)'), Roman et al. (2017) empirically retest only Experiment 2 of Eisenberg et al. (2002) (retained shipped input_row_index '622', DOI 10.1097/00003446-200210000-00007) using Eisenberg et al.'s (2002) noise-vocoded lexically easy and hard word and sentence lists. Kirk, Pisoni, and Osberger (1995) is cited in the Introduction as the earlier precursor for the easy/hard lexical manipulation that Eisenberg et al. (2002) adapted, is never tested or mentioned in Results, and is mentioned in a single Discussion commentary sentence noting that replicating Eisenberg et al. (2002) is also consistent with earlier results of Kirk et al. (1995). Under the codebook replication-chain and stimulus-precursor rules, the target retested by Part I is the closest study in the chain, Eisenberg et al. (2002) (input_row_index '622').

decisions.location: Materials and Methods, page 9, lines 503-516 (and Discussion, page 14, lines 782-794)
decisions.quote:
Noise-Vocoded Lexically Controlled Words and Sentences—The stimulus lists of
lexically controlled words and sentences originally developed by Eisenberg et al. (2002)
were used to investigate the effects of word frequency and neighborhood density on word
recognition in isolation and in sentences. Eisenberg et al. (2002) created two lists of words
based on lexical competition: one lexically “easy” list and one lexically “hard” list. Each list
consisted of 15 practice words followed by 60 test words produced by one female speaker.
The easy and hard word lists were then combined to create one set of 30 practice words and
120 test words that were noise-vocoded and presented in a randomized order. Practice trials
always preceded test trials (see PDF, Supplemental Digital Content 1). For the word
recognition task, children were instructed to repeat what they heard out loud to the
experimenter. No feedback was provided regarding response accuracy.
Eisenberg et al. (2002) also created two lists of 25 low-predictability sentences (5 practice
and 20 test sentences) using the same easy and hard words that were produced by one
female speaker and previously presented in isolation (see Bell & Wilson, 2001).
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In Part I ('Part I: Replication of Eisenberg et al. (2002)'), Roman et al. (2017) directly replicate Experiment 2 of Eisenberg et al. (2002) (retained shipped input_row_index '622', DOI 10.1097/00003446-200210000-00007) using the pediatric word and sentence lists created by Eisenberg et al. (2002). Bell and Wilson (2001) is cited in Methods as the adult sentence-materials precursor that Eisenberg et al. (2002) adapted and in a single Discussion sentence noting that the Eisenberg et al. (2002) replication results also parallel Bell and Wilson (2001) with adults, without any separate empirical test in Results. Per the codebook replication-chain and materials-source rules, Part I's retested target is already represented by shipped row '622' (Eisenberg et al., 2002).
